basis.text: Two commanders' reports of 1863 who were with the army's headquarters that night disagree by an hour: Meade (report of 1 Oct 1863, p. 115) says he reached the field at 1 a.m. of the 2d; Hunt (27 Sep 1863, p. 232) says the commanding general reached Gettysburg about 2 a.m. Howard and Stannard (reports of 1863) have him on the field riding the line at about 3 a.m.

default.label: Between about 01:00 (Meade) and about 02:00 (Hunt) on Jul 2; drawn at 01:00
default.basis_text: Lower bound: Meade's own report (arriving at 1 a.m. of the 2d, 1 Oct 1863). Upper bound: Hunt's report (about 2 a.m., 27 Sep 1863). Howard's and Stannard's reports of 1863 (about 3 a.m., Meade already there) and Haskell's letter (Meade on the road at midnight) bracket the window from outside.

animation.note: 01:00 is the earliest hour any first-hand writer gives for the arrival (Meade himself); Haskell's letter has Meade still on the road at midnight, so nothing earlier is source-supported. Hunt's about 02:00 stays selectable.

default.note: Meade's hour is his own arrival, but Hunt was in the same party; nothing in the record separates two reports of the same rank, so the window is shown and neither end is struck.

weighing.summary: Two reports of 1863, both by men at army headquarters that night, give different hours: Meade 1 a.m. (he left Taneytown at 10 p.m.), Hunt about 2 a.m. They are of the same rank (official reports written 87 and 91 days after), each by a man who was there, each on the Union clock; Hunt hedges with 'about', Meade gives a round hour. Nothing in the rubric separates them, so the class is irreducible and the default is the window between them. Howard and Stannard (about 3 a.m., Meade already arrived) fix the upper limit from outside; Haskell's letter (Meade rode by Gibbon's camp at midnight, on the way) fixes the lower limit; 'after midnight' (Hunt 1887, Pleasonton 1879) is only a lower bound. The later books that say 'at or just before midnight' name no source and are contradicted by Haskell; the plan's 04:00 has no source and is contradicted by Howard and Stannard.
weighing.who: Meade commanded the army and gives his own arrival; Hunt was chief of artillery at headquarters and says Meade 'soon after his arrival' sent him to see to the artillery, and in his article of 1887 writes 'we left Taneytown' for the party; Howard, Stannard and Haskell were on the field or at the Second Corps' camp; Pleasonton rode with Meade. Bachelder (1873), the editors of Battles and Leaders (1887), Minnigh (1892), the 1913 Life and Letters and the Vermont volume (1914) were not witnesses of the hour and name no source.
weighing.when: Meade wrote on 1 Oct 1863 (91 days after) and testified on 4 Apr 1864; Hunt wrote on 27 Sep 1863 (87 days); Howard on 31 Aug 1863 (60 days); Stannard on 4 Jul 1863 (2 days); Haskell in July 1863. Hunt 1887 and Pleasonton 1879 are 24 and 16 years after and give only 'after midnight'. The books of 1873-1914 are 10 to 51 years after.
weighing.where: Meade, Hunt and Pleasonton were in the party that rode from Taneytown; Meade says 'the field', Hunt 'Gettysburg', Pleasonton 'General Howard's head quarters on Cemetery Hill' The sources do not say that these are different spots, and none states that the hour differs by place; the one hour between Meade and Hunt is therefore not explained away.
weighing.how_knew: Meade: his own movements (own_orders). Hunt: present at headquarters, eyewitness of the arrival ('soon after his arrival, he directed me'), with 'about'. Howard and Stannard: they met Meade. Haskell: he saw the party pass. The later books give no basis.
weighing.clock: All the Union witnesses use the Union clock; the plan's note that the two armies' clocks differed by about 20 minutes plays no part (every witness here is Union) and no correction is applied. Meade's 'at 1 a. m.' and Hunt's 'about 2 a. m.' are round hours; the quarter-hour reading of a round hour does not close an hour's gap. The departure hours also differ (Meade 10 p.m. in his report; Hunt in 1887 about 11 p.m., the word before the hour being damaged in the text; a writer in the Official Records volume, p. 130, says 'as he states, at 11 p. m.'): the ride took one to three hours on any reading.
weighing.independence: Meade's report, his testimony, Bachelder, the Battles and Leaders caption and the 1913 book's 'as he states' all lead back to Meade's own hour and are counted as one line (the lower end is flagged single_source). Hunt's report and his article are one line (the upper end is flagged single_source). Together they make two groups for the window. Howard and Stannard are two independent reports of the 3 a.m. meeting. Haskell stands alone for the midnight passage. Pleasonton (1879) and Hunt (1887) are two postwar writers for 'after midnight'. Hunt, Pleasonton and Meade rode together and are not independent of each other's memory of the night. The later books that give one o'clock (Bachelder 1873 and 1864, Battles and Leaders 1887, Toombs 1888, the county history of 1886 in its summary chapter, Fitz Lee in 1878) name no source and are counted with Meade; the county history's two o'clock, in its chapter on the battle, is counted with Hunt. Both groupings are assumptions, not shown copying.

source_panel_text: Meade reached the field about 01:00 on Jul 2 by his own report; Hunt's report says about 02:00. Both are reports of 1863 by men at headquarters, so the record is divided by an hour and the window stands, drawn at 01:00. By about 03:00 Howard and Stannard had him riding the line. The plan's 04:00 has no source. Eight other values are listed.

pdf_default.note: About 01:00 holds as the lower end and as the drawn instant (Meade's own report). The plan's 'pre-dawn inspection' is also documented, in the dark at about 03:00 (Howard, Stannard, Hunt), though Meade's own inspection began at first light; the plan's 04:00 and the single hour are not the whole record, since Hunt says about 02:00.

first_delegated.note: About 01:00 and the first-light inspection hold as quoted. The first delegated default left Hunt's about 02:00 out as a mere scenario; two witnesses of the same rank disagree, so the default is the window 01:00-02:00 (still drawn at 01:00), class irreducible, tier documented.

what_would_change_it: A note, log or letter written on 1-2 July 1863 by someone with Meade (Butterfield, Williams, Biddle, Meade's own letter of 2 July) that gives an hour would settle between 01:00 and about 02:00. A page image of Hunt's report reading a digit other than 2, or a source behind Epperson's 04:00, or behind the 'midnight' of the later books, would change the window.
